title: Young Sheldon
synopsis: You're nine, Texan, and smarter than your physics teacher. The county science fair is in two weeks. So is your sister's volleyball game. You have to be in two places. Use your brain.

nodes.text: Meemaw makes pancakes. Mary makes coffee. Georgie eats his weight in bacon. Missy reminds everyone — twice — about her championship game. You are, as usual, calculating something at the table. Choose “Announce your science fair project at breakfast” and The Project Idea comes into view; choose “Wait until Dad is in the room” and the road bends toward Dad's Practice.

choices.text: Announce your science fair project at breakfast
choices.consequence: You choose to announce your science fair project at breakfast. By The Project Idea, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

choices.text: Wait until Dad is in the room
choices.consequence: You choose to wait until Dad is in the room. By Dad's Practice, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: You propose a low-cost neutrino-detection experiment in the family garage. Mary blinks. Meemaw says, 'Oh, sweetie.' Georgie asks if it has anything to do with bowling. “Pivot to something doable in a garage” draws you toward Tam's Plan; “Insist on the original idea” leaves Missy's Suspicion waiting on the other side.

choices.text: Pivot to something doable in a garage
choices.consequence: Constraints are also creativity. You choose to pivot to something doable in a garage. By Tam's Plan, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

choices.text: Insist on the original idea
choices.consequence: You insist on the original idea. It gets you to Missy's Suspicion, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: George Sr. is at football practice. You walk down with a thermos. He asks how school is. You tell him about Newton's third law. He says, 'Sounds good, buddy.' You feel, briefly, that he listens harder than he lets on.

choices.text: Pitch the science fair project to him
choices.consequence: You choose to pitch the science fair project to him. By Tam's Plan, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

choices.text: Ask him about the volleyball schedule first
choices.consequence: You ask him about the volleyball schedule first. It gets you to Missy's Suspicion, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: Tam, your best friend, sees your project sketch at lunch and immediately offers to help. He has, he claims, 'a guy at the radio shack.' He always has a guy. The distance between Mr. Lundy's Permission and Meemaw's Garage begins with the choice between “Form a two-person team” and “Keep it solo for purity.”

choices.text: Form a two-person team
choices.consequence: You choose to form a two-person team. By Mr. Lundy's Permission, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

choices.text: Keep it solo for purity
choices.consequence: You choose to keep it solo for purity. By Meemaw's Garage, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: Missy, sharper than anyone gives her credit for, asks if you're scheduling your fair around her game. You consider lying. You consider not lying. You consider the third option, which is silence. To choose “Tell her the truth” means meeting Mr. Lundy's Permission; “Promise to be at her game no matter what” sends you toward Meemaw's Garage instead.

choices.text: Tell her the truth
choices.consequence: You commit to tell her the truth. The road to Mr. Lundy's Permission is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

choices.text: Promise to be at her game no matter what
choices.consequence: Promise first, plan after. You promise to be at her game no matter what. It gets you to Meemaw's Garage, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: Mr. Lundy — your physics teacher — needs to sign off on your project. He is, sweetly, intimidated by you. You realize you can either smooth this with kindness or steamroll him. Everyone in Mr. “Compliment a real strength of his” draws you toward The Wiring Problem; “Present the project as if you're the teacher” leaves The Family Schedule waiting on the other side.

choices.text: Compliment a real strength of his
choices.consequence: You commit to compliment a real strength of his. The road to The Wiring Problem is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

choices.text: Present the project as if you're the teacher
choices.consequence: You commit to present the project as if you're the teacher. The road to The Family Schedule is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: Meemaw lets you set up in her garage with two conditions: no fires, and you have to take a snack break every two hours. The snacks include a Dr Pepper she will share, even though she always says she won't.

choices.text: Negotiate longer work blocks
choices.consequence: You negotiate longer work blocks. It gets you to The Wiring Problem, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

choices.text: Accept her conditions exactly
choices.consequence: You accept her conditions exactly. It gets you to The Family Schedule, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: Saturday morning. The detector's preamp keeps oscillating. You consider the problem. The problem considers you. Choose “Methodically debug” and Pastor Jeff Visits comes into view; choose “Let Georgie hit it” and the road bends toward The Sleepless Tuesday.

choices.text: Methodically debug
choices.consequence: You methodically debug. It gets you to Pastor Jeff Visits, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

choices.text: Let Georgie hit it
choices.consequence: Sometimes pets are right. You commit to let Georgie hit it. The road to The Sleepless Tuesday is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: You draw a Gantt chart on the kitchen wall. Mary makes you take it down. You redraw it on a poster board and prop it against the wall. She accepts the compromise. You add Missy's volleyball as a critical milestone.

choices.text: Show Missy the chart with her name first
choices.consequence: You choose to show Missy the chart with her name first. By Pastor Jeff Visits, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

choices.text: Show the chart to Dad for buy-in
choices.consequence: You show the chart to Dad for buy-in. It gets you to The Sleepless Tuesday, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: Pastor Jeff drops by for tea and to subtly check whether your project is, technically, blasphemous. You explain particle physics with charm. He leaves with a flyer for your fair and a slightly worried expression.

choices.text: Invite him as a judge
choices.consequence: You commit to invite him as a judge. The road to Missy's Game, Friday is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

choices.text: Keep the church gently at arm's length
choices.consequence: You choose to keep the church gently at arm's length. By Dad's Quiet Help, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: You stay up too late three nights in a row. Meemaw catches you. She sits in the garage with you anyway and reads the newspaper while you solder. Choose “Sleep at a reasonable hour from now on” and Missy's Game, Friday comes into view; choose “Keep pushing — fair is in three days” and the road bends toward Dad's Quiet Help.

choices.text: Sleep at a reasonable hour from now on
choices.consequence: You commit to sleep at a reasonable hour from now on. The road to Missy's Game, Friday is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

choices.text: Keep pushing — fair is in three days
choices.consequence: You choose to keep pushing — fair is in three days. By Dad's Quiet Help, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: The volleyball game is Friday at 7. The fair is Saturday at 9. The schedule, miraculously, allows for both. You make it to the game with a notebook in your hand. Missy spots you in the stands.

choices.text: Close the notebook for the whole game
choices.consequence: You commit to close the notebook for the whole game. The road to Saturday Morning is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

choices.text: Keep glancing at notes between sets
choices.consequence: You commit to keep glancing at notes between sets. The road to The Awkward Question is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: George Sr., who you didn't know noticed, shows up at the garage at 9 p.m. with a roll of duct tape and zero physics. He holds the wire steady while you solder. He says, 'I'm here. That's all I got.' It is, oddly, all you needed.

choices.text: Thank him directly
choices.consequence: You choose to thank him directly. By Saturday Morning, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

choices.text: Nod and keep working
choices.consequence: You nod and keep working. It gets you to The Awkward Question, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: The fair. Folding tables. Other kids' baking-soda volcanoes. Your detector hums politely. The county judge, who has a Ph.D. in something else but knows physics when she sees it, leans in. Choose “Demo the detector with no shortcuts” and The Ribbon comes into view; choose “Demo with the dramatic flourish you've practiced” and the road bends toward Tam's Speech.

choices.text: Demo the detector with no shortcuts
choices.consequence: Be honest about your data. You commit to demo the detector with no shortcuts. The road to The Ribbon is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

choices.text: Demo with the dramatic flourish you've practiced
choices.consequence: You choose to demo with the dramatic flourish you've practiced. By Tam's Speech, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: A different judge — an older man — asks you a question you suspect is meant to trip you up. You realize, mid-answer, that he is testing for confidence as much as content. The paths divide here: “Answer plainly and concisely” leads into The Ribbon, while “Answer with proof and humor” makes Tam's Speech the next reckoning.

choices.text: Answer plainly and concisely
choices.consequence: You choose to answer plainly and concisely. By The Ribbon, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

choices.text: Answer with proof and humor
choices.consequence: You commit to answer with proof and humor. The road to Tam's Speech is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: You win the county. The ribbon is blue and cheap and you put it on your refrigerator next to Missy's championship pennant from last night. The fridge, you decide, is a kind of family altar.

choices.text: Aim for the state fair next month
choices.consequence: You choose to aim for the state fair next month. By The State Fair Letter, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

choices.text: Take a week off before the next thing
choices.consequence: You choose to take a week off before the next thing. By Sunday Pancakes, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: Tam, at lunch on Monday, gives a small speech about how you didn't ditch him for credit. You blink. You hadn't realized the choice was a choice. Friendship, you discover, has options you didn't see.

choices.text: Tell him you'll always include him
choices.consequence: You choose to tell him you'll always include him. By The State Fair Letter, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

choices.text: Promise to choose better, on purpose
choices.consequence: You commit to promise to choose better, on purpose. The road to Sunday Pancakes is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: An envelope arrives — the state fair, with a small stipend. Mary cries a little. Meemaw cries a lot. Dad pretends not to. Missy says, 'Cool,' which is, from her, the highest honor. The Hallway, Quiet comes either way; its meaning changes with the difference between “Take the family with you to state” and “Take just Tam.”

choices.text: Take the family with you to state
choices.consequence: You commit to take the family with you to state. The road to The Hallway, Quiet is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

choices.text: Take just Tam
choices.consequence: You commit to take just Tam. The road to The Hallway, Quiet is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: Sunday after the fair, Meemaw makes pancakes that are, somehow, even better than usual. You eat three. You watch your family argue about a Cowboys game. You realize, with a feeling you can't yet name, that you are happy.

choices.text: Stay at the table an extra hour
choices.consequence: You commit to stay at the table an extra hour. The road to The Hallway, Quiet is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

choices.text: Go work on the next project before noon
choices.consequence: You go work on the next project before noon. It gets you to The Hallway, Quiet, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: After the fair, after the pancakes, you stand in the hallway with the ribbon in your hand and decide whose company state will be. The decision is, you realize, also a decision about who you want next to you when the next door opens.

choices.text: Pile in the station wagon together
choices.consequence: You pile in the station wagon together. It gets you to Cooper, the Family, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

choices.text: Just you and Tam, partners
choices.consequence: You commit to just you and Tam, partners. The road to Cooper & Tam is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

choices.text: Already plan tomorrow's experiment
choices.consequence: You already plan tomorrow's experiment. It gets you to The Long Road, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: You go to state with Mom and Dad and Meemaw and Missy and Georgie. The trip is loud, chaotic, and one of the best weekends of your childhood. You realize, again, that science is a profession but family is a country.
You and Tam go to state, sharing a hotel room and a stipend. You stay up late watching TV that isn't on at your house. You win second. You don't mind. Tam tells the story for years.

Years later, in graduate school, you'll think back to this Saturday. You'll remember the ribbon and the fridge and the volleyball game. You'll realize, with a small ache, that the science was always going to happen — the choice was who you would be while it did.
